whyThisMatters: If you can name the trick out loud together, you will spot it faster on your own — whether it shows up in a permit request, a vendor invoice, or a tracking alert. Today's riddles use the same patterns Operations sees every day.
rememberThis: This month gave these tricks a name — keep using them. STOP before you skip a sign-off or approve a change, VERIFY through your own known channel, then REPORT.

discussionPrompts: Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up — FAKE INTERNAL TOOL ALERT and AUTHORITY IMPERSONATION both use a scary-sounding message, but the source they copy is different.
Ask for a real example of an internal alert or vendor invoice that matches one of these terms.
Ask someone to explain SAFETY SIGN-OFF BYPASS in their own words, without using the term itself.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often mix up FAKE INTERNAL TOOL ALERT and AUTHORITY IMPERSONATION. Both use urgency and a scary-sounding claim, so people pick one when the riddle points to the other. The difference: a fake tool alert copies your own company's system; authority impersonation copies an outside official body like a port authority.

riddles.riddle: I say the supervisor is unreachable and ask you to skip the signed permit-to-work "just this once". What trick am I?
I am a dry-dock invoice that says the bank details changed, and I want payment before the vessel departs. What trick am I?
I look exactly like your fleet-tracking tool's own alert, but I give you only 5 minutes to re-login through my link. What trick am I?
I claim to be a port authority demanding an urgent fee to avoid detention, but I didn't come through your own PSC liaison. What trick am I?
I claim a commercial emergency and ask you to redirect the vessel's cargo, with no signed addendum. What trick am I?
I am the three-step habit: 1. STOP before you act, 2. VERIFY using a number or portal you already trust, 3. REPORT to the IT Service Desk. What is this rule called?
